EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 157) respecting the payment of certaiD railway subsidies. He said : This is a Bill to make it possible to fix the amount of a subsidy before the work is completed. Under the present law a subsidy of $3,900 per mile is contracted for, and under the terms of the Subsidy Act, if the cost of the
railway exceeds $15,000, an additional subsidy can be paid not exceeding $6,400 per mile. This Bill seeks to make it possible, at the request of the railway company, to have a contract entered into, upon the report of the chief engineer, for the payment of a fixed amount. The $3,200 would be paid on progress estimates, as at present, and 70 per cent of the cost above $3,200 would be payable, the remaining 30 per cent being held until the final completion of the work. The operation of the present' Act causes very much difficulty to the department and also to the Auditor General. He favours fixing the amount beforehand, upon a survey and report of the chief engineer, by the Minister of Railways and Canals under the authority of the Governor in Council.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon. CLIFFORD SIFTON (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 158) to amend the Land Titles Act of 1894. He said : The purpose of the Act is to enable the owner of farm land to register a mortgage under the Torrens system before he has secured the deed from the company from which he buys, such as the Hudson Bay Company, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or any other land company. Under the Torrens system in the Northwest Territories, an agreement for sale, or anything except an absolute transfer, cannot be registered. There is provision for the filing of a mortgage before the patent issues in the case of land granted directly from the Crown ; but when a farmer buys land from a company, unless he has the deed as the owner, though he may have paid the full price, he cannot register a mortgage on the land. In practice this is found very inconvenient owing to delays on the part of the companies in issuing deeds, and it is proposed to allow the registration of a mortgage on the filing of a certificate from the selling company that the land has 'been paid for in full. While I am amending the Act in this way, I am taking advantage of the circumstance to remove a technical defect that exists in regard to the registration of maps and plans.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the government whether there has been any correspondence with the imperial government respecting the exclusion of foreign vessels from the coastwise trade. My reason for asking the question is that I have seen some remarks of Lord Lansdowne which I observe reported in the ' Journal of Commerce and Commercial Bulletin ' of June 25. The report of the remarks of Lord Lansdowne in that journal reads as follows :
The noble Lord has called the attention of the House to a subject of the utmost importance, a subject which has attracted not his attention only, hut that of many others besides. He is correct when he cites a resolution at the conference of colonial premiers in support of his views, and he is also correct in reference to the report of the Subsidies Committee. The resolution of the colonial premiers has been referred to the colonial governments for their opinions. We have received some but not all of their replies, and these vary in their nature. Some of the colonial governments are entirely opposed to the idea of excluding foreign vessels from their coastwise trade, and others, on the contrary, are desirous or intend to do so.

Then Lord Lansdowne proceeds to deal with that subject at considerable length, as reported in this journal, but it is not necessary for the purpose of my question to quote the remainder of his remarks. I wish to know whether any communications have taken place between this government and the government of the United Kingdom with respect to the matter referred to. and if so, whether there is any objection on the part of the government to bring down such communications and place them before parliament.

Speaking on the spur of the moment I think, though I am not quite sure, that we have had some correspondence on that subject lately-in fact I am pretty sure we have. But whether the correspondence is in condition to he brought before parliament I could not say to-day. Perhaps I could oblige my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) later on.
Perhaps the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) would give us whatever information can properly be given to parliament on as early a day as possible.

What are the amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendments are not of very great importance. The Bill oi'-iginally provided that the Governor in Council might at any time in the interest of navigation appoint the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to be the pilotage authority for any pilotage district, that by Order in Council the pilotage authority might be changed to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The amendment made by the Senate is that the change can only be made :
Upon the recommendation of the shipping interests of the port or of the council of the board of trade.

FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved that the amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 102) to amend the Shipping Casualties Act, 1901-Mr. Prefon-taine-be concurred in.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. Would the Minister of Justice be good enough to state what these amendments are?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are four amendments which are not of very much importance. The first amendment is to section 1 of the Bill. Under the Bill as we have it now the expression ' pilot ' is defined in the following words :
The expression ' pilot ' means any person not belonging to a ship who has the conduct thereof.
To which definition the following words are to be added :
After ' thereof ' insert the following as subsection 2 :
2. The word ' pilot ' is inserted after the word ' mate ' wherever the expression ' master, mate or engineer,' occurs in the said Act.
The next amendment is in respect to the officers winch the government may appoint to make preliminary inquiries respecting shipping casualties. That section is amended so as to provide that the territorial jurisdiction of any such officer or person shall be defined in the appointment. Subsection 2 of paragraph 4 is amended by adding the words after the word 'default' ' or by the incapacity,' so that the section will now read:	.
If, upon a preliminary inquiry, the officer holding it is of opinion that any loss, or damage, or the stranding of any ship, or any loss of life, has been caused by the wrongful act or default or by the incapacity of the pilot in charge. &c.
The next amendment is to section 27 of the Act of 1901 which is section 3 of the Bill we are now considering. By the Bill as it passed this House it was provided that the court could fine
Any licensed pilot in any sum not exceeding one half of the net income he derives from his service as a pilot, based upon his earnings for the previous year.
The change is that of the words
One-half of the net income he derives from his service as a pilot, based upon his earnings for the previous year.
There are substituted the words :
Four hundred dollars and not less than fifty dollars.
Motion agreed to, amendments read the second time and concurred in.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to ascertain just what rights members have in this House when they ask for information which they deem to be of importance, and which they have a right to receive from the government. A few minutes ago I rose in my place to ask the Minister of Labour whether it was a fact that the Grand Trunk officials had been supplied from day to day with the official report of the evidence taken before Judge Winchester ; and I am in the judgment of the House when I say that having asked in the most respectful manner for that information, I was treated in the most boorish manner by the Minister of Labour. It was suggested that in asking for this information I was making a statement that I had no foundation for making, and that charge I resent. The Minister of Labour has been long enough in this House to know how to conduct himself as a gentleman. and to respect the rights of others. I wish now to ascertain from the Prime

Minister if I was not within my rights in what I did ? On the basis of a statement from Mr. Geo. L. Griffith, provincial secretary of the Dominion Institute of Amalgamated Engineers, I asked the question. That statement, dated Winnipeg, 14th of July, is as follows :-
The Grand Trunk Pacific officials have been supplied daily with a copy of the evidence by Judge Winchester's stenographer on instructions from the Minister of Labour.
That statement was mailed to me by the gentleman who has supplied uot only the Minister of Railways, but the Minister of Labour and many hon. members on both sides of the House, with information respecting the allegation made in the first place, as to the employment of alien engineers, and respecting the conduct of the inquiry. Upon the strength of that statement I was quite within my rights in asking for information. I protest that my courteous questions were not treated in a way that I had the right to expect they would be treated. I do not desire to occupy the time of the House, except to say that so long as 1 have the honour of a seat here I shall strive to conduct myself in as courteous and gentlemanly a manner as possible ; but neither the position which the Minister of Labour occupies nor the length of time he has been in this House will save him from castigation if he does uot treat hon. gentlemen as they have the right to be treated by him.

I am sorry that my hon. friend the Minister of Labour is not in the House at the present moment to answer the charge that has been brought against him by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke). I do not think that my colleague is liable to any censure in this respect. As I remember the incident, my hon. friend from Toronto asked whether or not the Grand Trunk officials had been supplied from day to day with a copy of the evidence, and the Minister of Labour answered that he was not aware that anything of the kind had taken place
speakername: Sir WILFRID LA UR IK  II@

speechtext: Might I remind the Prime Minister that the Minister of Labour asked once or twice what I was insinuating.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour stated that he was not aware that any such information had been given to the Grand Trunk Company, and my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) was surprised, because he evidently anticipated an answer to the contrary. The hon. gentleman pressed the point and thereupon my colleague stated that the hon. gentleman was misinformed, that Judge Winchester had no such instructions, and that he was not aware that such a thing had taken place. I may further say that in the relations between gentlemen on both sides of the House, there is I believe an effort to carry on these relations in a gentlemanly manner, and I am quite sure Mr. CLARKE.
that the Minister of Labour would be the last to be guilty of any boorishness-I do not think that was the proper word for my hon. friend to use. We are all human and liable to get hot, and probably in this very hot weather it is hard to keep cool.

Statements have been made to me to the contrary, of what the Minister of Labour would lead the House to believe. I am not presuming to pronounce judgment upon what the true facts may be, but I will read the statements that have been made to me from the same source which has been mentioned. This letter is from the Secretary of the Society of the Amalgamated Engineers, and it says :
Although 'copies of our letters to the government department were immediately forwarded to Mr. C. M. Hays, a similar courtesy was not afforded to us. The various communications of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway did not reach us until the second return sessional papers No. 124 ordered by parliament was brought down and a typewritten copy sent to us.
Further :
We respectfully asked the Minister of Labour to allow His Honour, Judge Winchester, to supply us with a typewritten copy of the evidence taken before the commission so that we could intelligently follow the investigation and render assistance, but our request was refused, although Mr. C. M. Hays and the Grand Trunk Pacific officials were supplied with typewritten copies of the evidence daily.
I do not know whether that is correct
or not, but that is the statement made to me and I am informed that a similar statement has been made under date, July 14tli, to the Minister of Railways.
Is that the same question that was up before this morning ?

I will repeat the extracts I have read for the Postmaster General who was not present. I have stated that I do not know whether the statements are correct or not, but they do not appear to be in harmony with the views of the Postmaster General.
I recognize the writer of that letter as Mr. Griffith.
I so stated.

As to the statement that his letters to me were furnished to Mr. Hays whilst a similar courtesy was not extended to him ; that is incorrect. In any case where I transmitted a copy of Mr. Griffiths' letter to Mr. Hays I did the same to Mr. Griffith. I made no distinction between either of the parties to the case ; I was desirous of getting at the facts ; I wanted to see where the truth was. Mr. Griffith was charging-and as the facts have disclosed very correctly charging

that United States engineers and others had been

employed, aud Mr. Hays was not giving us that information that I thought the circumstances entitled us to. There was a withholding of testimony so that it was impossible to determine what the facts were. During the whole of that correspondence which I was conducting with Mr. Griffith and Mr. Hays, in order that each one should know what the pther was saying to me, I deemed it my duty to transmit to the one the copies of the other's letters so that they would know what case was to be answered. Mr. Griffith was treated with every courtesy; just as much as Mr. Hays was. With reference to the statement that he applied to the department to furnish him from day to day with a verbatim copy of the evidence ; this was after the inquiry had begun and when it was proceeding at Winnipeg. The department had no machinery for furnishing the public with verbatim copies of the evidence. The meetings were public, the press was represented. We had one stenographer to take down in shorthand the evidence. I should be amazed to learn ; I am as satisfied as I am of my existence that there is not a scintilla of truth in the statement, that any officer of the department furnished verbatim or other copies to the Grand Trunk Company or to any other body. I am perfectly satisfied that it never occurred, but the stenographer is here and I will make inquiry at the department, and I will answer the hon. gentleman later on that point.
That is perfectly satisfactory. I have no knowledge of the truth of the statement, but I thought it advisable to bring it to the attention of the hon. gentleman.
I am satisfied that it is an unqualified mistake.

But I would hardly regard this society as in the position of the general public, so far as its right to receive the evidence is concerned, because it is the body which brought the matter to the attention of the government. Therefore I would suppose that any facility of that kind might very properly be furnished to it.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIv. They were in attendance, and any one who read the Winnipeg papers would see that the evidence was taken down aud published very fully by them-in some instances as fully as it was taken down by the stenographer-and every facility was afforded to them to know everything that was going on. Mr. Winchester invited co-operation, and no step could be taken by him that would in my judgment in the slightest degree promote a more efficient inquiry than has been held.

My hon. friend has stated that there was a communication sent to the Minister of Railways' similar to the
one which he has received from Mr. Griffiths.
I said I am so informed. I have no knowledge of it myself.

I may say that up to Saturday night I had not received any such communication, and so far as I have been able to go through my letters this morning, I found none. My correspondence was very voluminous, and I have not been able to open all my letters which have come in the mails since Saturday night; but if there is any such communication, I will bring it to the notice of my hon. colleague, the Minister of Labour.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to place before the House a grievance in connection with the tobacco industry of Canada. I mentioned a few days ago to my right hon. friend the leader of the government that I would avail myself of this opportunity to place before the House certain facts connected with that industry, and I will proceed to do so as briefly as possible, concluding by moving an amendment to this effect:
That the government has not given the tobacco industry of Canada the protection and encouragement it is entitled to.
I think I shall be able to demonstrate that that industry has been neglected in a culpable degree by the government, in spite of the repeated representations made to the government in various forms, by deputations, by memoranda, and by correspondence. In fact, the day after I had given notice of this motion to my right hon. friend, my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. L. P. Brodeur), gave notice of a resolution, the object of which is to remedy, at any rate in part, the grievance complained of, which is proof, I think, that the government has been remiss in its duty to this industry. I will refer to that resolution briefly as I proceed with the examination of this question. I will content myself with giving summarily to the House the information which I deem absolutely necessary to a proper understanding of this question, without which the House could not really appreciate the motion which I propose to move.
It may not be known to all the members of this House, though it is known to many, that the tobacco industry is one of great interest to a large number of people in Canada, and that the culture of tobacco, which has received an increased amount of attention in the last few years, is extremely remunerative. Therefore, anything connected with that branch of agriculture ought to interest us to a very large degree. The culture of tobacco, as it lias been carried on by many of our people in different parts of

Canada, is susceptible of yielding from $120 to $150 an acre, and even more. If you get from an acre, properly cultivated, 1,200 or 1,500 pounds of tobacco, which is sometimes obtained, you will receive for it at a moderate estimate 10 cents per pound. Consequently tobacco culture is one of the most remunerative kind ; and if proper means had been taken to encourage that culture and the domestic trade in our own homegrown tobacco, as well as the foreign trade which that article is susceptible of obtaining, we would have done a great deal to enrich the farmers who give themselves up to this culture in different parts of the country. In the province of Ontario, tobacco is principally cultivated, I believe, in the county of Essex ; but in my own province it is cultivated pretty extensively everywhere. In the counties of Montcalm, E'As-somption, and one or two others in their vicinity, the culture of tobacco is very extensive. It has been remunerative, and it is susceptible of being made still more so if the means suggested to encourage its cultivation and trade are adopted. It is cultivated to a considerable extent in my own county, and in other counties around the city of Montreal. In some instances where the culture has been carefully attended to, the results have been really phenomenal. So that the matter deserves the attention of the House as regards both the manufacture and the cultivation. Perhaps I had better proceed to mention at once what are the present duties upon tobacco. The customs duties on tobacco, cigars and cigarettes are $3 per pound, and 25 per cent ad valorem ; on manufactured tobacco and snuff, 50 cents per pound ; on cut tobacco. 55 cents per pound. The article is also susceptible to a very considerable rate of excise duties, which I will briefly give to the House. The excise duties are as follows : On foreign manufactured tobacco, 25 cents per pound ; on Canadian home-grown tobacco, 5 cents per pound ; on combination tobacco, that is, tobacco proper, partly of Canadian leaf and partly of foreign leaf, 5 cents per pound. Then, there is an excise duty which is in reality a customs duty, but which for purposes of convenience has been made collectable by the Department of Inland Revenue because that department has greater facilities for apportioning this particular duty properly, calculating the moisture of the tobacco and its proper weight. On raw leaf, foreign tobacco, there is an excise duty of 10 cents oer pound ; on stemmed raw leaf, scraps and cuttings, foreign tobacco. 14 cents per pound. I think that is the only original duty which has been imposed by the present government upon tobacco. The other duties to which I have referred existed previous to the present government coming into power. On cigarettes made from foreign leaf there is an excise duty of $6 a thousand ; on cigars made from domestic leaf, $3 a thousand ; on combination cigars, that Mr. MONK.
is, cigars made partly from foreign and partly from home-grown tobacco, an additional excise duty of 16 cents per pound ; and on combination cigarettes, an additional excise duty of 37J cents per pound.
On combination cigars made from stemmed tobacco and scraps and cuttings of tobacco, a still further duty of 23 cents per pound, and combination ^cigarettes made partly from stemmed tobacco, imported into the country, and partly with homegrown tobacco, an additional duty of 53 cents per pound.
In connection with combination tobacco, the [DOT] nature of which I have already explained, there are still further duties. Combination tobacco from foreign leaf is subjected to a duty of 20 cents per pound additional and combination tobacco made from stemmed foreign leaf, 23 cents additional. These special duties imposed upon combination tobacco have been so calculated as to impose upon tobacco made partly of foreign leaf and partly of native leaf, a measure of duty based upon the duty imposed on pure native tobacco and the duty imposed on foreign tobacco separately.
There is a duty on snuff tobacco, moist, of 18 cents and dry, of 25 cents.
There are still further duties which I feel I should mention so as to put the House in full possession of the state of our tariff as regards the article in question. There are still further duties on cigarettes as follows :-Foreign cigarettes not more than 3 pounds per thousand, a duty of $3 per thousand; foreign cigarettes, weighing more than 3 pounds per thousand, $8 per thousand ; Canadian cigarettes, that is cigarettes made purely of Canadian tobacco, $1.50 per thousand ; combination cigarettes, made partly with foreign leaf and partly with native leaf, $1.50 per thousand.
These duties which I have just explained in detail to the House result from the legislation passed in chapter 19 of 60 and 61 Vie., being legislation to amend the Inland Revenue Act and moreover in virtue of Orders in Council dated 1st July, 1897 and 19th of June, 1903. The object of these Orders in Council was to apportion in an equitable way the duties to be imposed and collected upon combination tobacco. Therefore I understand that what the present government has done, that is what constitutes its own legislation so to speak, is the imposition of a duty on the foreign leaf of 10 cents and a duty of 14 cents imposed on the stemmed leaf. There is also to be credited to this government the apportionment of the duties under the Orders in Council which I have just cited, and the excise duty upon combination tobacco in such a way as to collect the duty in a reasonable way upon the foreign ingredients in the combination tobacco and also upon the home grown leaf entering into its manufacture. Having stated the legislation

that has been passed upon this subject, I deem it necessary to lay before the House the result of this legislation since the past few years. I shall begin with a statement of the quantity of tobacco manufactured in this country in the three classes of imported, Canadian and combination tobacco.

All the figures that I have given are from page 82 of the report of the Department of Inland Revenue for 1003. I gather from these figures that the quantity of imported tobacco has diminished in recent years,while the quantity of home-grown consumed is greater. The reports indicate that the quantity of home-grown has improved, and the country, although consuming a great deal more tobacco than formerly, has imported less of the foreign tobacco and has used a greater quantity of native growth. This is a fact that is not generally known, but which it is necessary to make known in order that we may appreciate the motion that is now before the chair. In view of these important facts, it is understood, those engaged in the culture and manufacture of tobacco have represented to the government on several occasions and in a variety of ways, as by petitions, deputations and so on. that it is now absolutely necessary to do something more than has been done hitherto to foster and protect that industry. It is necessary, in order to give that most remunerative culture and industry the encouragement that is deserved, to take additional means to ensure its still greater development. The principal points submitted to the government and upon which tobacco manufacturers and growers have made representation I may mention in their order, and briefly that I may not take up too much time.
In the first place, the industry has represented to the government most emphatically that it is necessary to adopt legislation in order to suppress the monopoly of the American trust, the American Tobacco Company. It is known that at present we are threatened ' throughout the. country, and particularly throughout the province of Quebec and large centres like Montreal and Quebec with the absolute monopoly of the tobacco trade, a monopoly which, as I am informed. can be traced to the great American tobacco trust which is represented here by two Canadian associations incorporated an-

der our own law, but which in fact, represent the American tobacco trusts ;-I refer to the American Tobacco Company and the more recently incorporated Imperial Tobacco Company. Conceiving that that monopoly is injurious to the trade and has a tendency to curtail the trade and to centre it all in the hands of this monopoly, the tobacco manufacturers have made representations to the government in order to have it abolished. Conceiving also that ultimately the monopoly will affect the tobacco growers of Canada as it will finally place in the hands of the monopoly control of the entire output of tobacco in Canada, the tobacco growers also have protested against this monopoly. The government, on several occasions have had deputations wait upon them, and, to some of these parties they have promised to put an end to the monopoly by legislation. In fact, last session, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) in pursuance of this introduced an amendment to the criminal law having for its object the abolition of that monopoly. That amendment which was calculated to meet the existing difficulty, was abandoned. It is true that an amendment of an analogous nature has been introduced by my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Brodeur) since I gave notice that this subject would be brought up for discussion ; I will say a word about that amendment before I resume my seat. The tobacco industry has asked, further, as a means of encouraging this remunerative industry a moderate increase in the duty upon imported tobacco. I believe the deputation asked for an increase of ten cents per pound on foreign tobacco and fourteen cents per pound on the foreign manufactured article. This small increase is necessary under the British preference, for the great American tobacco trust has now more or less transferred the seat of its operations from the United States to England. We receive from England, particularly in recent years, very large consignments of tobacco, the property of this trust, which is sold here far more largely than before, under the rebate of the British preference, and at reduced cost of manufacture, I believe. In the third place the industry has asked for the use of a uniform stamp upon all tobaccos whether imported or not. The reason for that is that the green stamp used for Canadian tobacco solely, as experience shows, has the effect of rather impeding the sale of Canadian tobacco. As everybody knows there is, in some quarters a certain prejudice against the home-grown tobacco, and the colour of the stamp has the effect of preventing the sale of the homegrown tobacco.
I believe there are at the present time three stamps used by the Department of Mr. MONK.
Inland Revenue, a black stamp, a red stamp ' and a green stamp, put upon the Canadian 1 products. What they have asked is merely that stamps of a uniform colour may be used, and the testimony of all those versed ' on the subject is that it would be a great advantage in an indirect way to the cultivation of Canadian tobacco. They have asked in addition something which I think is of very great importance, and without which the industry to which I am referring cannot really prosper satisfactorily in this country. They have asked for the establishment-in connection with our experimental farms, I presume, would be the cheapest manner-of experimental stations where tobacco growers could obtain profitable information as regards the cultivation of tobacco, both for home and foreign market. Those acquainted with the subject know that our home market is insufficient, while there are large markets abroad for our tobacco which we can obtain with a little effort, there is no doubt whatever about that. They have therefore asked for these experimental stations conducted by the government itself, in order to encourage the cultivation of our own tobacco. Furthermore, they have asked for the establishment of a bureau of information in order to keep those engaged in the tobacco culture fully informed of the requirements of the home and foreign markets, exactly as is done at the present moment by the publication of bulletins by the experimental farm. The Central Experimental Farm gives the farmers information, both as regards the improvement of the growth of the products of their farms, and also in regard to the markets, domestic and foreign. There is no doubt that our tobacco growers, if information were carefully prepared by the government and given out to them in bulletins from time to time, could greatly improve and increase the output of tobacco.
Not long ago an important deputation came to Ottawa from my own province and laid all these matters very fully before the government. Without going fully into the details of their representations, i may say that the deputation was introduced to the right hon. the Prime Minister and to my hon. friends the Minister of Inland Revenue and the Minister of Finance. They asked for a small increase in the duty, they asked for a uniform stamp, for the reason I have stated, the establishment of experimental stations, the establishment of a bureau of information and for a law to put an end to the tobacco monopoly now in the hands of a trust. The deputation was introduced by my hon. friend from L'Assomption (Mr. R. C. Laurier). I find that the counties of Montcalm and L'Assomption were very well represented on that deputation by leading men, and among other delegates I may mention Mr. Wilfrid Legault and Mr. Claude, of the parish of St. Lau-

rent, in the county of Jacques Cartier, and there were gentlemen from other parishes. Mr. Legault is engaged in the manufacture of tobacco at St. Laurent, and has taken a very active part in the representations made to the government.
Now I wish to submit that the government has not acceded, so far as I can see, to a single one of those requests, though the government has repeatedly recognized the justice of those demands and representations. Now in regard to the monopoly, the government assured those who wished to put an end to it, that the moment the existence of that monopoly and its injurious effects were established, that moment legislation would be introduced to put an end to that monopoly. Judge McTavish was appointed by the government to hold an inquiry in order to ascertain-I believe that ' was the restrictive scope of the inquiry- whether such a monopoly existed. I moved last year for a copy of the report of Judge McTavish. It contained many interesting details in regard to the existence of this monopoly, but I will not take up the time of the House in referring to them fully. As a matter of fact, the finding of Judge McTavish was that the monopoly did exist. In hifi report he gives us the text of the contracts that are made by the American Tobacco Company with dealers, with what we call jobbers in tobacco, and the text of the contract which the Imperial Tobacco Company makes with the jobbers in cigars and cigarrettes ; and he arrives at the conclusion, which is very clear, in the light of the texts of these contracts and of the accompanying testimony given in the investigation, that the monopoly exists, and that it is impossible for those who deal in the goods of the trust to do so with any prospect of profit except by conforming to the exclusive regulations of the monopoly. The American trust has secured the very best brands of tobacco, the best brands of cigarettes and the brands that have most favour in the market, and nobody can obtain a sale of these articles from the company except by signing this contract, which has a monopolistic effect. Judge McTavish therefore arrives at the conclusion that the monopoly really exists. It has the effect, says the judge, of restricting the trade to a few hands. He was not able, nor had he instructions, to inquire as to whether it injured tobacco growers, but I think he says in his report that it must ultimately have that effect. Judge McTavish points out that in the state of Massachusetts where a similar evil exists, legislation has been passed to put an end to it, but that was so recently that he had not been able to find out what were the results. Well, that inquiry having been made and the report laid before the government, it became the duty of the government to introduce legislation to put an end to what they admitted themselves was an evil. Last year the Minister of Justice, as I have already stated proposed to add article 520a to the Criminal Code in the following terms :

That amendment, introduced by my bon. friend the Minister of Justice, acting, I presume, from the conviction obtained by the government from this commission that the evil existed and that it was necessary to put a stop to it, remained a long time before the House last year and was ultimately dropped, for what reason I do not know. I know that some question was raised as to the effect this amendment might have on other lines of business that bad been subject to close scrutiny, but it might have been restricted to the tobacco industry, since the evil existed and since the bon. Minister of Justice and the bon. Minister of Inland Revenue had promised faithfully that the evil would be remedied. The measure was dropped, and. as I stated a moment ago, the bon Minister oif Inland Revenue, after I bad given him notice of my intention to bring* this subject before parliament, introduced a measure of an analogous nature which I do not think goes far enough. My bon. friend, in his proposed amendment, which is embodied in the resolution now before the House-
Mr. BRODEUR, Does my bon. friend think this is a proper opportunity to discuss this amendment ? I do not think it would be regular on a motion to go into Committee of Supply to discuss the subject of a notice of motion.

I am not discussing that motion itself, but I am discussing the nature of the remedy which it is evidently the intention of the government to apply in regard to this complaint. I do not intend to dwell

at any great length upon it. We will discuss it when it comes up in regular way, but what he proposes is to give the lion. Minister of Inland Revenue the right, if he finds the condition of things to exist which is pointed out by Judge MacTavish in his report, which is alleged by those who complained to the government and which is described in the proposed amendment introduced last year by the lion. Minister of Justice, to withdraw the license from the licensed manufacturers who have a contract of that kind ; in other words, since the evil exists, since it has been recognized by the government, instead of applying the bare remedy which the government had promised to introduce, the Department of Inland Revenue has the power, if it finds that a monopoly exists, as it lias been proved to exist, to' withdraw the license from one of the licensees or one of the manufacturers. I will say at once to my hon. friend that I would rather see that done than nothing at ail. The government should have the power at any time, if sufficient pressure Is brought to bear upon it, to put an end to the evil in that way, but what I submit to the House is that it leaves the hon. minister the sole judge of the extent of the evil.
I would like to Know where the hon. gentleman gets that information, because I do not see anything of the kind in the resolution of which I have given notice.
This is the resolution of which my hon. friend gave notice on Friday last
There is nothing mentioned about the Inland Revenue Department or the Minister of Inland Revenue.

This is what it says :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Inland Revenue Act, in providing that :
(2.) Any license authorized by this Act may be cancelled in any case where a person who, being a manufacturer of any class of goods subject to a duty of excise, either directly or indirectly-
Then follow the clauses of the amendment introduced last year.
It does not provide that this power is vested in the Department ol' Inland Revenue or in the Minister of Inland Revenue.

It is vested in the government, at any rate. It is an amendment of the Inland Revenue Act, and I suppose that any action that is taken to put this amendment into force would have to start with the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue. Probably it would require to be confirmed by Order in Council, but all I mean to say is that instead of curing the evil, as was promised last year, this is simply legislation having for its object to allow the government to cure the evil if it sees fit to do so Mr. MONK.
This is another example, among many which I have known since I became a member of this House in 1896, of the government taking into its own hands power which, I submit, ought to be exercised by parliament alone. This is in regard to the great grievance which exists and which the government has often been requested to put au eud to. Now, as a matter of fact, and as I think the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue is aware, the trust or the monopoly has not remained idle since the holding of the inquiry by Judge MacTavish, but it has gradually increased its hold upon the trade, and it is threatening to get possession of the whole tobacco trade of Canada, in so far as the manufacture of tobacco, cigars and cigarettes is concerned. I find that the output of cigarettes in 1902 was 137,000,000, and that the American Tobacco company sold of this number 109,000,000 in Canada. Since 1901, I think it is admitted that the trust has seized hold of the manufacture of Canadian leaf under the name I have already indicated, of the Empire Tobacco; Co(hi-pany, and by lits exclusive contract, to which I do not like to refer at any greater length, but which is amply set forth in the report of Judge MacTavish, it is gradually getting hold of the whole business In tobacco, and it is a mere question of time when this huge corporation will be able to control absolutely the output of Canadian tobacco. Not only is that the fact, but those who are largely interested in tobacco growing and those engaged in the manufacture of tobacco, who are not dependent on the trust, and there are among these a great many experts, agree that that is the result to which we are tending now.
I do not think the government has a satisfactory record so far as the monopoly is concerned, and it Is evidently because the government had a feeling of contrition and compunction, that, when they saw this question was going to be referred to in parliament, they judged fit to introduce the mild remedy of which the Minister of Inland Revenue gave notice last Friday. The government has refused to give any additional protection to the tobacco industry. All those Interests in that industry agree that a little additional protection would be necessary, but the last deputation that came here to get additional protection was told by the 'government that it was too late this year, thereby giving them to understand that probably additional protection would be afford-'ed at a later date. It is admitted on all hands that some additional protection would not diminish the revenue because the slightly increased rate of duty would amply compensate for the diminution of importations if such diminution would follow. Moreover, we must have foreign leaf in this country and Canadian leaf cannot by any possibility totally displace it. Even the most sanguine and enthusiastic supporter of the Canadian tobacco industry does not ad-

vance the pretention that the public demand will be satisfied with Canadian leaf alone. Canadian tobacco has been Improved it is true, and we can send a great deal of it to foreign markets, but we cannot prevent the importation of the foreign leaf which Is absolutely required in this country. There would therefore be no diminution of revenue and it seems to lie admitted that the increase in the consumption of the commoner kind of tobacco would be a great help to the inative industry. The demand of those interested, made to the government, that there should be uniformity in the stamps placed on tobacco is a most reasonable one. Dealers and growers have represented that the distinctive green stamp on Canadian tobacco creates a prejudice against it, and impedes its sale. They, therefore, ask that stamps of the same colour be used for all kinds ;of tobacco, and I do not think the government has given any sufficient reason why this demand should not be acceded to.

The Speaker of the House of Commons.

Did time permit, I should be very glad to he permitted to go further into Judge MacTavish's report, and I would have been pleased to read certain letters which I have received from tobacco manufacturers and tobacco growers in the province of Quebec, strongly urging the views which I am endeavouring to impress upon jthe government. I now shall say a few words upon the refusal of the government to establish experimental posts in compliance with the request made by those who have experience in the matter. I shall also refer to the absolute neglect of the governmnt to establish a sort of information bureau for [DOT] the growers of Canadian tobacco, and which could be established at small expense. The government is in possession of a petition signed by all the influential people interested in the tobacco industry in my province,
,and which promulgate the views of which I have given a brief resume. Neither the report of Judge MacTavish, not this petition, which bears one thousand signatures, nor the very important report of Mr. Blaise Dugas have been printed and circulated for the information of those interested in the industry as they should have been. Mr. Blaise Dugas, whom I do not know personally, but who is, I am told, an expert, was sent to Belgium two years ago to obtain complete information on the possibility of there being a demand for Canadian tobacco on the European market. That report ot Mr. Dugas, which I moved for in this House .was brought down on the 27th day of May last. I do not wish in any way to minimize the importance of the scant information contained in Mr. Dugas's report, but I say that he supports very strongly the argument that I am advancing for the information of the government. However, Mr. Dugas's investigation was very incomplete and very superficial Tfie information contained in his report as to the value of the Belgium and Dutch market for our tobacco is of little practical use. Had the government sent over samples of our tobacco with instiuc-tions to our representatives in London, Paris and Belgium to make a report, an equally good result could have been obtained at much less cost. The fact, however, that the government did send over Mr. Dugas proves that strong pressure had been brought to bear and that the ques-tiou deserved greater attention than the government had seen fit to give to it. Mr. Dugas took ten or twelve packages of tobacco with him; he submitted'them to some leading dealers in Antwerp, London. Liverpool. Glasgow and elsewhere, and we have his views as to their opinions.
What is important is this-and it will no doubt surprise the House-that this tobacco. taken principally from the counties of L'Assomption and Montcalm, not cured, not packed, not prepared as tobacco should be in order to obtain a favourable reception in European markets, was most favourably received by those who were privileged to examine it. I do not wish to take up the time of the House by reading extracts from Mr. Dugas's report; but if the government sees fit to have it printed, as it undoubtedly should be, members of the House will at once see, to their surprise, I am sure, that in England there is a very good market for our tobacco. The merchants who were consulted by Mr. Dugas are men of great responsibility, commendable in every way ; and from the observations they made to him it is evident that in the markets of England, Scotland and Ireland, which consume over 100,000,000 pounds of tobacco a year, there is a good opening for our tobacco, provided that proper attention is given to the cultivation of the plants, the curing and the packing. Now, summing up the observations of the Belgian, Dutch, Liverpool, Glasgow



and London tobacco dealers. I venture to [DOT]say that they all agree that the samples which they inspected, which were brought over by Mr. Dugas would, with improvement, constitute a very good tobacco for sale on the British and continental markets. It (appears, from the observations of these gentlemen, what most of us know, that what we require is not only an improvement in the cultivation of the tobacco, but proper training in regard to curing and packing it. But if these needs are provided, we have an unlimited market open to iis in England and on the continent. In order to secure .these ends it would be necessary for the government, as Mr. Dugas recommends in his report, and as all those who have any knowledge of the subject have earnestly urged upon the government time and again, to have some experimental stations. Members of the House will be surprised to hear, for instance, that most of the tobacco that is used in Belgium is grown in Wisconsin. The Americans have opened an immense market for their tobacco all over Europe ; but they have spent far more than $30,000,000 in acquiring the necessary science in the cultivation of tobacco, and the curing and packing of it, to suit that great market. That is for us a very important point, because our market is strictly limited. The counties of Essex and Kent in Ontario, and the principal counties in the province of Quebec where tobacco culture is carried on furnish a sufficient supply for the needs of our own country ; but if we had the means of introducing our tobacco upon the markets of Europe, a very much larger area might be cultivated with extraordinary success. Mr. Dugas, as I stated a moment ago. makes the suggestion in his report, that we should have experimental stations.
I think these could be secured in connection with the existing experimental farms, the central farm and its branches, at a trifling cost ; and it is impossible to appreciate the .extent of the returns. In regard to the curing, there is no doubt that we would have to obtain the services of two or three experts from the United States, men conversant with th'e needs of the European markets. That would not be a very great expense, and most excellent results would follow. In order to do that I venture to say that our Minister of Agriculture would have to take a little more interest in the affairs of his department and a little less perhaps in the affairs of other departments; for, after all, with what great agricultural reform or progress has the Minister of Agriculture associated himself during his incumbency of the office ? It was for a time boasted that he had invented cold storage ; but everybody knows that the merit of the establishment of cold storage does not accrue to the Minister of Agriculture. He has merely perpetuated what he found when hie came into office, and I venture to 'Say that when the estimates of that hon.

Conservative regime. In 1896 there were twenty-seven factories engaged in the manufacture of foreign leaf. In 1903, there were only twenty-three of such factories, a reduction of four. Let us see how during the same period the factories engaged in manufacturing domestic leaf progressed. In 1896 there were only ten factories of domestic leaf, and last year that number had been increased to thirty, including those engaged in the production of combination tobacco. So, while we have decreased the number of factories of foreign leaf we have increased very largely those engaged in the manufacture of tobacco, of Canadian growth. In 1896, the tobacco manufactured from foreign leaf amounted to 9,609,191 pounds. In 1903, the last year for which we have the reports, the quantity had decreased to 7,726,316 pounds,-a decrease of 1,182,778 in the manufacture of foreign leaf to-day as compared with what it was under the Conservative regime. Now, take the figures for the Canadian leaf. Hon. gentlemen opposite, when in power, would not give any protection to the Canadian leaf ; they would not do anything for the Canadian farmer. The result was that, when they were in power, in 1896 we manufactured only 474,205 pounds of Canadian tobacco. Last year we manufactured of Canadian tobacco no less than 4,983,181 pounds, an increase in the manufacture of Canadian tobacco of 4,463,376 pounds. In 1896 the quantity of Canadian tobacco manufactured in the form of cigars was 515,870 pounds, making a total manufacture of Canadian tobacco in that year of 990,075 pounds. If we estimate this tobacco at ten cents per pound we find that the Canadian farmers received for their tobacco $99,007.50. Last year, 1903, besides the 4,938,181 pounds of Canadian manufactured tobacco, we used for cigarettes. 2,300,081 pounds and for cigars 9,598,890 pounds, a total of 16,837,052 pounds, as against 990,075 pounds under the Conservative regime. Take this total quantity at ten cents per pound, and we find that last year the farmers of this country with the protection they enjoyed from this government, received for their tobacco, $1,683,705.20, or $1,584,697.70 more than they received in the last year of the Conservative regime. There is the result of the policy of the government. And I cannot understand how, in the face of results like these, my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and hon. gentlemen opposite generally can complain of that policy. But is it fair to say that all hon. gentlemen opposite complain of the policy of this government ? Some time ago I heard my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) speak words which indicate that he does not share the views of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier. $14,000,000 to $16,000,000 ? They could get clear of a large portion by extending the reduction of duties from molasses to sugar. They could also make a reduction in the duty on tobacco, which would prove an immense boon to almost every man who contributes to taxation.'

Is it the hon. meui-ber for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) or is it ' the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) who has a right to enunciate the policy of the opposition since he is its financial critic? I am sorry he is not in his seat to-day ; but I suppose when the vote comes on he will be here to tell us on which side he stands. But that is not all. The government has not given to the tobacco industry of Canada the protection and encouragement that it is entitled to.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have shown by the figures I have just read that instead of having neglected the tobacco industry this government has done it's best to develop it. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier says that the preference is affecting tobacco imported from England, and that when it is manufactured by the American Tobacco Company in England it would be subject to the preference. I suppose my hon. friend has not read for some time the clause in the statutes relating to the preference. My hon. friend must have forgotten that part of the statutes relating to the preference, as otherwise he would not have made this argument in connection with tobacco imported from Great Britain. We have a right to expect now that my hon. friend will repudiate the statement that he lias made that the duty on tobacco imported from Great Britain is not the same as on tobacco imported from foreign countries. Now. Mr. Speaker, we have been in favour of a duty for the protection of the Canadian industry, we have also made a change which has been very beneficial to that industry; Before 1896 the Canadian growers and manufacturers asked our friends opposite several times to permit the mixing of Canadian tobacco with the foreign leaf. Several petitions to that effect were presented to the Conservative government, but in every instance they were refused. When the liberal party came into power we permitted the mixing of Canadian tobacco with the foreign leaf, and the result has been a very large increase of the Canadian consumption of Canadian tobacco. In 1895-96 no cigars were manufactured in this country from mixed tobacco, but in 1902-03 we manufactured 6,660,330 cigars. So far as the tobacco itself is concerned, we had none in 1895-96, but last year we manufactured 1,772,974 pounds. So you see, Mr. Speaker, that this policy of permitting the mixing of Canadian tobacco with foreign tobacco has been fruitful, has given the best results and has contributed to a large extent to the increased consumption of Canadian tobacco. The reason for that is easy to understand. You cannot put on the market a very good brand of cigars unless you use a wrapper of the finest leaf. In the United States they generally use Sumatra leaf for wrappers and in this country they also use Sumatra to a large extent. By permitting the use of Canadian tobacco with foreign tobacco we enable the manufacturers to put into the inside of the cigar Canadian leaf which is just as good as foreign leaf and then wrap this tobacco with Sumatra leaf. The result has been that whereas formerly we were manufacturing very few cigars we are now manufacturing them by the million.

The session is drawing to its end and it was important that notice of this amendment should be given as soon as possible.

The reason for adopting this procedure is very obvious. The question has been asked as to why we should not meet this condition by an enactment in the Criminal Code. the policy declared last year by the government, declared to some extent by myself on the 15th of June last, and declared by the notice which I gave the other day.
MyJhon. friend, speaking on the question of tobacco, said that we should provide for ifniformity in stamps. He asked for a declaration of policy on the part of the government in regard to that subject. There is much to be said in favour of having a uniform colour of stamps for foreign and Canadian tobacco. I had thought at first that this question might be solved simply by departmental regulation but I find that it cannot be dealt w'ith very conveniently in that way and that if treated in that way it' would not prevent frauds upon the revenue. The best way to deal with this question would be by legislation and it may be dealt with by providing different scales of duties applicable to different kinds of tobaccos. There is not unanimity among the Canadian tobacco manufacturers in this respect. Some are in favour of the change while others, and perhaps the most prominent ones, are opposed to a uniformity of stamps because they believe that Canadian tobacco is gaining such a reputation for its quality that before long it will be in very great demand. I was about to say that in spite of the increased duty on foreign leaf, the Canadian consumer is now paying less than formerly for this tobacco, as the figures will prove. In 1896 he paid for domestic plug chewing tobacco 81 cents, and this year he pays 53 cents for the same quantity of tobacco.

speechtext:
Yes, I suppose it is the Jsame kind. I am not a smoker, but I am told by those who do smoke, that Canadian tobacco is very much better than the foreign tobacco. My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) apparently does not accept that statement, but I make it on the authority of a gentleman who changed from foreign to domestic tobacco, and he now says that the Canadian tobacco is the better. When hon. gentle-inen opposite become more Canadian than they are now, they will perhaps give up the foreign leaf and smoke our own good Canadian product. T.et me continue to quote the figures. In 1896 plug smoking tobacco cost eighty cents when it now costs fifty
cents, and in 1896 foreign smoking tobacco cost $1 when the smoker can now get the same quantity for forty-six cents. In these three kinds of tobacco the consumer is now paying in one case fifty-three cents less, in another case sixty per cent, and in the third case seventeen per cent less than he did formerly. And why is this the case ? It is because instead of smoking foreign leaf tobacco which is pretty heavily taxed, the consumer now smokes Canadian tobacco on which the tax is only five cents per pound. The net result of the policy of the government is that we have given to the Canadian producer a large amount of protection which encourages the growth of tobacco in Canada to the value of $1,500,000 more than under the Conservative regime, and at the same time we have reduced to a very large extent the price of the tobacco itself.
. Mr. CLANCY. Was it the policy of the government, of which the Minister of Inland Revenue is so distinguished a member, in raising the duty on tobacco to especially encourage the growth of Canadian tobacco in Canada.

subtopic: PUT THIS IN YOUR PIPE AND SMOKE IT.
speechtext: Certainly that was the purpose and intention. The purpose was to favour as much as possible the growth of Canadian tobacco, and the figures I have quoted prove that the policy of the government in this respect has been a sound policy, which ought to meet with the support of hon. gentlemen opposite.

speechtext: I congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) sincerely, that by the introduction of this motion he has drawn from the government the first clear honest distinct and manly statement in favour of a pijotective policy, that I have heard since I came to parliament. I congratulate the Minister of Inland Revenue for casting aside the hypocrisy of his party, and in a manly way stating his own policy in reference to this question. If members of the government would always admit that they looked with horror upon their past and promised to do right things in the future, I would cease to berate them, and would endeavour tio help them on in their career. I believe that in the end Canadian tobacco will be found to be of the most superior quality, because every product that can be grown in this northern country is of the highest excellence. We grow the best men and women in file world, and the country that grows the best men and women will grow every inferior product in the highest excellence. What are the Ontario members doing in this debate ? Do they know that in 1890 their province raised 11.000,000 pounds of tobacco, and that last year it raised only

'3,000,000 ? it would seem from these figures as if the policy of the government was helping Quebec, while it was destroying poor Ontario, and yet there is not a man of them opposite who seems to be aware of the condition of the tobacco industry in that province. I recently searched through the reports of the Dominion stati-tistician and I discovered that in 1902 we raised 500 pounds of tobacco in Nova Scotia, 30,000 in Prince Edward Island and 61,000 in British Columbia. There are no returns from Quebec, but I suppose Quebec is so much on top now that it need not be mentioned in statistics. In 1896, Ontario raised 11,000,000 pounds of tobacco leaf, mostly in the county of Kent and Essex, while in 1902, the last year for which we have returns, it only raised 3,000,000. I do not understand how this result can come from the policy of the government, because if they afford adequate protection it is bound to strengthen the growth of tobacco all over the country. No man who has seen the benefits of protection as conferred upon the United States of America can doubt that a wise system of protection would encourage Canadian industries. I congratulate the Liberal party in coming around to that sane view.
I was somewhat surprised however, that 'the Minister of Inland Revenue, who is somewhat liberal in his views, should attempt to make a little political capital out of this question. He should remember what befell the Postmaster General a few days ago, who, when he was discussing the Peterborough lock tried to introduce a political issue, and before he got out of it he was the worst whipped man I have ever seen in the House of Commons. I thought the Minister of Inland Revenue had more discretion ; I thought he had the French discretion, never to attack until he was sure to win ; I thought he had the Napoleonic genius to win or retreat, but he seems to have been off his guard this afternoon. Why the Conservatives could not hold by the policy they had. Such were the continued and persistent attacks of the Liberal party that the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Foster, showed awful weakness in going back from his policy of high protection and making sugar and several other articles free. What happened ? From that day I lost confidence in Foster-in everybody connected with the government. It did much to defeat the Conservative party, because the opposition told the people that the government had never believed in their policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Did I correctly understand my hon. friend to say that he lost confidence in Mr. Foster because of the action he took in connection with the tariff in 1896 ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What has he to say about the gentleman who wrote the leaflet on tobacco which he read a moment ago ?

I am coming to the leaflet. I say I lost confidence, and I am frank in that. There is nothing like frankness among friends, and I say the Conservative party showed awful weakness in betraying their party by giving into you people-giving into your endless talk about things you never believed in for one moment-instead of going on building np and strengthening their tariff. They would have been in power to-day if they had done that instead of playing into your hands. You evidently do not intend to be defeated by any of your free trade nonsense, because you are abandoning every shred of it and throwing it to the winds, and adopting protection. My hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue is the advance guard in declaring that the old policy of the Liberal party is gone forever, and that protection, pure and simple, is its policy to-day. I want to tell the Minister of Finance, when he goes to Nova Scotia, not to wear the mantle of hypocrisy which he has worn so long, but to throw it off and to appear in the costume which the Minister of Inland Revenue has put on and worn so worthily to-day. With regard to that circular, I do not think the Minister ot Inland Revenue should have pursued the course he did. In this country-and unfortunately we have many illustrations in the province of Quebec-there is a class of people who are always advocating a sectional policy. >I know nothing about it. I have been brought up in an atmosphere where that humbug could not last for a moment. I admire the French Canadian people in many ways, and I wonder that they have not a man strong enough to take those people who are talking sectionalism and shake the life out of them, as Chapleau did the people who were talking sectionalism at the time of Riel. It is a pity they have not a strong French Canadian who would do the same thing to-day.
Haven't you got Mr. Tarte ?

The proof of the pudding is in the eating of it, and when I see people in Ontario licked into being national men instead of sectional men, I want to see a big, powerful man in each province able to destroy sectionalism of every kind. However, I was going to say that I think it unfair that the Minister of Inland Revenue should have brought that little bit of a circular into this discussion. I venture to say it was written in Ontario or Quebec.
If my hon. friend will tell me who published the circular, I will withdraw my speech.

I have never read or seen it; but I say it was very wrong for a minister of the Crown to attempt to read a

circular which has no authority, so far as 1 know, and which does not bind me or anybody else. Probably no man in this House ever saw it. Some man who wished to earn a few pennies writes something which he thinks may be in the interest of his party or the country, and the Minister of Inland Revenue brings it forward to bind the great Conservative party. It binds nobody and deceives nobody. It does not dignify the debates of parliament to introduce matters of that kind. It is a good tu quoque argument, if arguments of that kind are to prevail in Canada. It may do to catch somebody at a public meeting, but it does not mean anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How about the hon. member for Pictou ?

He has a right to inveigh against surpluses if he wishes, and if his constituents believe in that kind of thing. I believe we should have far more surpluses in this country ; but we should spend them in the development of the country. l7ou people are afraid of expenditure , you are not attempting to develop this country at all. We want two or three thousand miles of railway in Nova Scotia, and you will not build any. The whole country is undeveloped to-day, while you people are piling up surpluses. I do not object to surpluses, but I object to your not spending them in the development of the country, but giving them to your friends and encouraging boodle.
But my hon. friend must see that the hon. member for Pictou was advocating a reduction of the duty on tobacco.

Yes, he did specifically mention the subject of tobacco. Well, my hon. friend has been here ten or fifteen years, while I have been here only four years, and he may have got impregnated with the notions which you people have been preaching. I have not ; I steel myself against them ; and you have so improved in your conduct that we perhaps need less will-power to do so now. But even a man of good sense who was here before 1896, and who listened to the distinguished men leading the opposition talking the twaddle they did for ten years, might have lost some of his intellectual virility, and Mr. Bell may have suffered in that respect. However, I support the hon. member for Jacques Cartier in advocating a strong duty to give the Canadian tobacco-grower absolute protection against all comers, until he shall get his industry into that state when he can face the world alone. I believe the time will come when the Canadian will face the world and conquer it in a fair field of battle. But this is not the moment ; w-e have not the capital, nor the skill, nor the training. I support the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, and I say the Minister of Inland Revenue will not be able to convince the people
of Quebec that it is a sufficient answer to his argument to quote a circular written by nobody, and representing nobody's views ou this side of the House that I know of.
It was mailed from this House to members of parliament
That does not bind anybody. Suppose you mailed a warrant to hang me to-morrow, that would bind nobody.
What about the franking of it ?

People have a right to send any material they like to the country. That is a very weak argument. If my hon. friend has taken the correct course the people of Ontario should be up here inquiring seriously into the question how their province has been deprived of this industry. This industry has been stricken down from 11,000,000 pounds of tobacco to 3,000,000 pounds in three or four years. That is a question for the people of Ontario. You stand jeering and laughing at the quibs and jokes of the Minister of Inland Revenue which would be very timely and appropriate in addressing school boys. He did that well but I am sure that he fancied he was addressing School boys rather than serious men or he would have produced arguments more timely and suitable than those which he advanced. The reason I desire some information about the province of Quebec was to find out whether a similar loss had occurred in that province. In Ontario the industry has declined from 11,000,000 pounds to 3,000,000 pounds, and if there had been a similar decline in Quebec it would fully justify the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I am attempting to master the beautiful language which my hon. friend speaks as his mother tongue, and when I do master it I am going to the province of Quebec to ask the people of that province whether it was sufficient answer to the charges of my hon. friend Jacques Cartier for the hon. the Minister of Inland Revenue to read to the House a circular which he found somewhere.

It is rather refreshing to hear the Minister of Inland Revenue declaring the new doctrine of the Liberal party. He has now become quite a protectionist. In answer to my question he declared in unequivocal terms that it was the policy of the Liberal party to give protection to the tobacco interests, to encourage the growth of tobacco in Canada and that for that reason the increased duties were imposed in 1897. I think I understood the hon. gentleman to say that in the most unequivocal terms.
If my hon. friend will permit me, what I said was that the policy of the government has had for effect to encourage the production, the growing of Canadian tobacco.

Then I have not misunderstood the hon. gentleman. Has the hon. gentleman forgotten that he has marched In the ranks of the Liberal party for many years declaring that protection had ruined the farmers ? Have hon. gentlemen forgotten that they went up and down the back concessions declaring that when the Conservative party imposed duties upon every article produced by the farmers of Canada these duties were utterly worthless to help the farmers of this country ? Does he deny that that was the policy, the doctrine, as preached by his own party-and by himself as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) suggests. When did he become convinced that farmers should have more protection ? Let me read to my hon. friend what the Minister of Finance said when he introduced the revision of the duties in 1897. The hon. minister should have consulted the Minister of Finance before he made his statement this afternoon.

I would like to inquire of the government whether the report of the Commissioner of Fisheries with regard to the dog-fish pest and other matters, has been laid on the table of the House. I observe that elteven weeks ago to-day the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) stated, in

reply to a question from the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Raulbach), as follows:
1.	The Commissioner of Fisheries was authorized to hold an investigation into the dog-fish pest and other fishery matters on the shores of northern New Brunswick. The investigation concluded on April 21st.
2.	The report is in preparation, to be laid before me in a few days.
3.	The report referred to is awaited before deciding the question of a dog-fish bounty.
4.	A large number of suggestions are before the government, and steps will be taken when the report referred to is presented.
I have inquired more than once of the officers of thle House, and I cannot find that this report, which was to be brought down within a few days, on the 2nd of May, has been brought down yet. I would like to inquire the cause of the delay.

speakeroldname: Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: At the time that answer was made it was expected that the commissioners would meet and prepare their .report. Some members of the commission are members of this parliament, *nd unfortunately they havle been unable to attend to this question during the sitting of the House. Their preliminary report is not yet ready, but I will make inquiries and see whether it is possible to have it down before the vote is taken.

I may say to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that it seems a littile surprising that a report rwhieh at that time was to be presented within a few days has not been presented after eleven weeks. I suppose the constitution of the commission was known as well then as it is now. The minister has mot referred to any unexpected circumstances, or any cause which would seem to me sufficient to justify the delay. It is of great importance that this report should be brought down. I have had many communications on the subject, and I have desired more than once to address the House on the subject, but I have waited from time to time until the report should be brought down, because it seemed unadvisable to enter into a discussion when we were daily expecting the report. I would ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether he has any idea, any expectation that the report will be laid upon the table of the House in time to havte a discussion on the subject before the conclusion of the present session. It is a matter of very great importance indeed to the fishermen of the maritime provinces ; it is one which has attracted a great deal of public attention there and elsewhere, and it is highly important that this report should not be longer delayed, unless there is some very grave reason for it. Therefore, I would ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to expedite this report, and let I
us have it within a day or two, if possible. The answer which I have read did not mention any others of the commissioners, but referred to the fishery commissioner only. It was said that he was making an investigation, and would be prepared to make his report almost at onefe, which would be laid on the table within a few days. Now my hon. friend refers to some other members of the commission who are not mentioned in this answer at all. I see no reason, for my part, why this report should not have already been before the House.

As regards the commissioner of fisheries, Mr. Prince, I may say that we have already in the department an exhaustive report from him on that question. The question has been taken up, not only by himself but by the other members of the commission who sat during last winter, investigating this matter as well as some others. In the department we understand perfectly well that this is an important question, and it is be-jcause of its great importance, and the great number of suggestions that have been made to us, some contradictory of each other and others tending to involve the government in a very heavy expenditure, that we are studying this question very carefully before we make a report which would be practicable. At the present time I do not think that any of the suggestions made to the commissioners have been found practicable. Of course it is only reasonable that they should confer together before coming to a conclusion. I will inquire to-morrow of the commissioner of fisheries whether he is in a position to make, if not a complete report, a temporary report on the question. We do not ignore the importance of the subject, and when the papers are before the House the hon. gentleman will see that we have been dealing with it in earnest, and the volume of correspondence and information which has been gathered will show that we have neglected nothing.
Who composes the commission ?

So far as I 'remember, it is composed of Mr. Prince, Col. Tucker, Mr. Copp, Mr. Armstrong. Mr. Bowers, and one or two others whose names I forget at the moment. They were appointed a few days after the close of last session.
Have they been engaged ever since in making a report ?
They have made preliminary reports on other questions, but on this, the most important of all, they have not yet made a report.

speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Labour if he has sent his deputy minister to Montreal to investigate the circumstances of the Italians who have arrived in that city and are said to be in destitute circumstances. Has a report been made to him, and if so, when will it be laid on the table of the House ? It is also stated in the press that this matter has been referred to Judge Winchester to investigate and report upon, and can the hon. gentleman give us any information on that point ?

subtopic: C931 COMMONS ITALIAN IMMIGRANTS AT MONTREAL.
speechtext: I sent the Deputy Minister of Labour to Montreal to endeavour to ascertain how these Italians that were reported to be stranded in Montreal, came to Canada. He endeavoured to ascertain the facts, but he found a great deal of conflicting testimony. He came to some conclusion upon the subject, but I cannot say that he 'made a report, because the testimony was contradictory, so much so, that I recommended to Council, in order to get at the facts, that Judge Winchester's commission should be enlai'ged so as to embrace this subject. Accordingly his commission was enlarged, and I expect that Judge Winchester will begin to investigate this subject as soon as he is through with the inquiry in regard to alien labour troubles in Montreal, Judge Winchester is to-day in the city of Montreal. I am most anxious that he shall first complete the inquiry into the Grand Trunk alien labour question, and the moment that is done, he will take up ithe other question!, perhaps during the present week, but on that point I am not quite sure.
