When this matter was under consideration on a former occasion the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) promised to bring down the instructions given in regard to the survey of Walpole island. Perhaps the hon. gentleman has that information now.

speakeroldname: Hon. CLIFFORD SIFTON (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will give the hon. gentleman a statement of what is taking place :
On the 22nd December, 1900, the authority of His Excellency in Council was obtained to spend $2,250 and $750 from the capital funds respectively of the Chippewas and Pottawat-tamies of Walpole island for surveys. The reason for making the expenditure is stated bo be the impossibility of proiperly administering the lands and roads unless the islands are properly surveyed. Instructions were issued to G. W. McC-corge, Esq., of Chatham, on the 13th September, 1901, a copy of which is attached. When the attention of the department became known, the Indians petitioned that the work be not undertaken, alleging as a reason that their funds would not bear the cost. The department having used the argument that it was intended for their benefit and would undoubtedly lead to good results and a more businesslike administration of their property, a memorial was received in June last from the chiefs and councillors representing the chief agricultural Indians of the island, requesting to have the survey proceeded with. The surveyor has done some preliminary work, chiefly laying out the road allowances about the island and tracing the internal, roads, and .'picking up the points of the lands of the Indian locatees.
I have an extract from the letter of the surveyor which substantially gives instructions which were given to him.
The hon. gentleman might state shortly the plan upon which the survey is to be made.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The instructions given were as follows :
The Indian holdings as they now exist are to be surveyed and permanently posted, making only such necessary changes as may be required to straighten boundaries and this should not be done without the concurrence of the chief and councillors and the owners of the holdings affected. If any such change is objected to and you think it is very desirable, you should by argument endeavour to remove the objection. Wherever possible the rear boundaries of two or more holdings should be one straight line. For this purpose additions'may be made to the holdings.
The present roads should be made as wide as possible up to and not exceeding 66 feet in width. They may be diverted, changed or closed as may be decided on consultation with the agent, chief or councillors. All new road allowances should be 66 feet wide.

That is the plan in substance.

What provision is there for lands unclaimed ? The hon. gentleman knows that there is a very considerable quantity of land which is neither occupied nor claimed, and when the holdings are surveyed there will, of course, be a considerable quantity of land which is neither occupied nor claimed. The department have no doubt taken into consideration what the effect of the survey under such circumstances will be.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The instructions further provide that :
After the Indian holdings are surveyed and posted, you should lay out the remainder of the lands in double fronted concessions. The loits should contain 80 acres. The distance therefore across a concession of regular width will be 80 chains and the width of regular lots 20 chains, allowance for side roads should be made where considered advisable ; generally not nearer than every five lots.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The practice is to seize the timber and compel the parties to pay double dues and costs. In cases where timber is valuable and that penalty would not be adequate, we take the timber away from them altogether and proceed for other penalties as well.

ill'.* SPROULE. I am told that it is a common practice to take Indian timber, and that often the department knows nothing about it. The ordinary value of timber is far more than double the dues, so that 'such a penalty is not adequate.

I have always held that that punishment was no adequate punishment whatever, and as evidence of that, I cite that fact that the same men have been punished in the same way more than once, and have gone and done the same thing again.

speechtext: In the case of the maritime province Indians the position of the government is just this. /We simply have to exercise a sort of paternal supervision over them, and have to do the best we can in each case as it arises. But, where there is a case of distress, the distribution of seed grain and so on is carried out, and this must be largely at the discretion of the agents. No hard and fast rule can be adopted, and more than a hard and fast rule can be adopted for the relief of distress in Ottawa.

What is the condition of the Indians there that they should be differently treated from those in the other provinces? This is an old settled province. Have the Indians been taught habits of industry, and have they learned to farm or carry on any other productive labour? What is the reason for this condition on the part of the Indians ? It surely cannot be lack of opportunities for employment. Is the difficulty in the administration ? There must be something wrong. Perhaps the hon. minister will explain the condition and tell us why these Indians should be distinguished from other Indians under apparently similar circumstances.

When they put in their little crop they move about from place to place sometimes making butter tubs, sometimes barrels, and so on. Then, when the hay is about fit to be cut, they move back to their little farms. The crop that they raise they feed to their few cattle and horses. I am intimately acquainted with the habits of the Indians in my own county.

That is hardly an explanation. These people are supposed to be able to sustain themselves. So, while this may seem a fairly large appropriation for the purpose of giving assistance, we cannot be said to do anything that is to be regarded as supporting the Indians. The government does not assume that duty. We simply give assistance where we think it absolutely necessary. In Ontario the circumstances are somewhat different. Some of the Indian tribes in Ontario have valuable lands and have settled down and become farmers, and are quite independent. SBut the Indians in Nova Scotia have not taken to farming to the same extent, and, while they do not receive very much more from the government, they do receive some more. I do not think the conditions can be improved at present. The difficulty lies in two things-in the first place the Indians have not land of a character to support them ; and in the second place, they are of a roving disposition, and my hon. friend knows that it is utterly impossible, in the case of a tribe that has the habit of roving to induce them to settle down.

Are the Indians improving in their farming operations, and are they indulging in farming operations to a greater extent each year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I think I may say there has been a very great improvement in the last few years. The improvement depends almost entirely on the character of the agent. We have some agents who are extremely successful and some who are not. We have from time to time to change our agents around. We find that one agent is not getting along -well with a band, that he is not suited for the work which he has assigned to him and we make a change. We have had to make quite a number of changes recently. The greatest improvement that has been made in connection with the agencies in the Northwest Territories, which are under the charge of Mr. William Graham at the File Hills. He has been in the department for a number of years. He took charge some years ago and he was very successful with the Indians in the File Hills, with the result that the Indians upon that and one or two neighbouring reserves raised 65,000 bushels of wheat. He has been so successful in connection with cattle raising that we are buying a considerable number of heifers which we require for the Indians on the reserves in his inspectorate. We have made him an inspector which will enable him to extend his work to the whole inspectorate. Mr. Markel has lately been promoted to the inspector of the western division and it is hoped that he will be able to bring about a very great improvement m connection with the farming operations ot the Indians in Alberta. There the Indians have very fine reserves and great scope for carrying on the business of cattle raising, and it is expected that we will be able in a short time to make them become self supporting as a result of the work that will be carried on under Mr. Market's supervision. Upon the reserves that have been in charge of Mr. Graham the improvement has been so great that we have ceased to distribute rations to the Indians as was formerly the custom. In Manitoba the improvement is not so marked. The scope for improvement is not so great there. That is a remarkable statement. Several years ago I brought this to the attention of the minister. When the printing trade was being done away with in the industrial school a printing p'iant was left on the hands of the government. A Mr. Thompson desired to
lease this plant from the government for the purpose of conducting a paper. He had many advertisements contracted for by the tradesmen of the town and the government agent there leased the plant to Mr. Thompson with the stipulation that he could cancel the contract by giving six months' notice. Thompson, however, was to have the first option of purchase. In a few months Thompson was notified by tile Indian commissioner that at the end of six months his contract would cease. He desired to purchase the plant, but the government refused to sell it and it turned out that the reason was they had arranged with Garrison, the editor of a Liberal paper in Virden, to take over this plant. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Just a word with regard to what the hon. gentleman (Mr. LaRivieret says as to the general question of policy. Whatever may be deemed desirable or otherwise, the fact of the matter is that the Indians own these lands just as much as my hon. friend (Mr. La Riviere) owns any piece of land for which he has a title in fee simple. The faith of the government of Canada is pledged to the maintenance of the title of these Indians in that land. Under the arrangement that we have made with them, our faith is pledged that we will not disturb them in the occupation of the land which has been reserved for them, except upon

their own consent being given in a specified form. We follow the policy of getting the consent wherever we can when we think it will not interfere with the means of the livelihood of the Indians ; for we realize, as my hon. friend does, that it would be to the interest of the Indians that the land should be thrown open for settlement and sold, and that they should be paid the interest on the proceeds rather than keep the land while putting it to no use. But my hon. friend recognizes the fact that we have to proceed in a diplomatic way and get the Indians to surrender their lands when they are willing to do so. The officers oi the department, having constant dealings with the Indians, know how far it is safe to go in each particular case. In the case to which my hon. friend refers, that of the Roseau reserve, after urgent requests had been made by the settlers, with some difficulty the inspector, Mr. Marlatt, I think it was, secured the consent of the Indians to sell a portion of that reserve. Under the law, the Indians are entitled to be paid in cash ten per cent of the proceeds of the land sold for distribution among themselves. I presume that the original intention of putting that in the statute was to offer a sort of inducement to the Indians to sell, for the Indian, like some wliitemen, has a fairly good appreciation of cash in hand, and the fact that they were going to secure something might be an inducement to them to surrender, when possibly they would not surrender if they were not going to get something immediately. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I- could not off-hand give the hon. gentleman the exact statistics.
I just want the hon. gentleman to state generally.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Speaking generally the result has been that the pupils of the industrial schools have not been able to go out in ordinary life and compete with white men. I have stated my opinion as to what was the result and what was likely to be tlie result of this form of Indian education. I itm perfectly satisfied that you cannot take the child of the ordinary prairie Indian, put him in the industrial school, keep him there until he is twenty-one years of age and turn him loose to make his living amongst white men. He has not the physical, mental or moral get-up to enable him to compete. He cannot do it. The result has been that to a large extent the Indians who have been educated in this way have gone back to the reserves. I do not think that this work has been in any way lost because I can say to my hon. friend from my own knowledge, having lived in the Northwest since 1S76, that there is the most marvellous change in the general character of the Indian bands.

Is that the result of the Infusion of educated civilized Indians into the reservation ?
Ml-. SIFTON. I think that is very largely the result of the educational work that is being carried on. I think we have got less per dollar from the money we have expended in the industrial schools than we have from any of the other schools. I believe in the day and boarding schools. We have got a great deal more for the money which has been expended on these schools. While we have not educated them to such a high point, we have infused a great amount of education amongst a larger number. Avery promising experiment is being made by Mr. Graham, the inspector of the Qu'Appelle agencies, who has been most successful in bringing about a better state of affairs amongst the Indians under his charge. He has made good practical farmers out of them ; they raised 65,000 bushels of wheat last year ; we are buying cattle from vhem for supplying other reserves ; they are most successful, and we have ceased the distribution of supplies amongst them. Mr. Graham has adopted this plan: He has set aside locations on certain portions of the reserve, and he encourages the young men and the young women who come from the schools to marry and settle down upon these locations. He endeavours to see that they are not interfered with by the rest of the Indians. As a matter of practice, one of the most serious difficulties in improving an Indian band is that just as soon as an Indian couple show an inclination to thrift and gather a little property around them, all their Indian relations think it is not necessary for them to work just in proportion as this couple is prosperous. Their relations

take their supplies, ancl consequently they have no encouragement to accumulate property. Mr. Graham has been most successful in this experiment. A few years ago I put him in charge of three different agencies and lately I have promoted him to be inspector, so that he has a larger scope for his activity. I believe Mr. Graham will solve the problem if it can be solved, and he will solve it by endeavouring to promote settlement in a separate locality of those who come from the schools, and where they can have as much higher type of civilized life than they could if they settled amongst the other Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not a bit. We are not a particle further than we were before. When I last spoke about it in this House my hon. friend will remember that I went to an enormous amount of trouble and a good deal of expense to get the matter in to shape, and we were in a position to make a bargain with the Indians, but unfortunately we could not come to terms with the then local government. The local government at the last moment set up a claim which made it impossible for us to carry out the arrangement. I am quite prepared at the present moment to carry out the proposition I made then, but unless the local authorities are willing to co-operate with us we are unable to act. I am quite prepared to instruct the officers to go on and carry out the proposition made then, but unless they co-operate we cannot do that. I am satisfied that if the local government would join in the proposition I made some years ago it could be carried out.
I noticed some time ago that the local government had taken steps to select a site for the Indians and that there was a possibility of the matter being settled.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They have not given us any advice as to that.
Indians-Yukon-relief and medical attendance, $8,000. '
Mr. W\ J. ROCHE. That is an increase of $3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The number of Indians actually located in the Yukon Territory is estimated at 702. The expenditure for destitute Indians for 1902-3 was $6,118.40, but accounts remaining unpaid on the 30th of June would bring this to over $8,000.	1
may say that we have no Indian service in the Yukon and we simply spend this money under t.he direction of the commissioner of the territory. In connection with the vote of $5,000 to provide education for the Indians of the Yukon, I may say that last year we spent under this head $2,029.66. The department has not established any per capita rate for boarding schools or day schools within the territory, but last year gave a total grant in consideration of cer-Mr. SIFTON.
tain educational work being done in the district. The work is principally carried out by the Church of England at Forty-Mile, Caribou Crossing, Selkirk and Moose-hide. The number of pupils enrolled at these schools is 100. The most important school is at Forty-Mile and is a combination of day and boarding school. We have not put up any buildings, but simply give the Church of England a small grant for this work.
Indians generally, P- H. Bryce, medical inspector, part of salary, $1,000.
This item requires explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The increase is caused by the appointment of Dr. Bryce, late secretary of the Ontario Provincial Board of Health. I have appointed him as chief medical inspector of the Department of the Interior and Indian Affairs. A portion of liis salary, $2,200, is charged to the department of the Interior, and $1,000 to the Department of Indian Affairs. The intention is that his time shall be divided between the two departments, and this $1,000 is therefore charged against the Department of Indian Affairs for the time he devotes to its service. The intention is that Dr. Bryce shall take a tour of inspection and endeavour to improve the medical attendance and the sanitary arrangements on the various Indian reserves. Hon. gentlemen who have taken any interest in the discussion of Indians affairs from year to year, particularly in the discussion of medical attendance on Indian reserves, must have observed that this question came up repeatedly. It was largely in consequence of these discussions and the opinions I formed upon them that I decided to endeavour to bring about some improvement in that direction. While we. have an efficient service as far as medical attendance is concerned, tfhere was a lack of supervision by a medical authority ; the only supervision that was possible heretofore was given by officers in the department who are not medical men and therefore I thought it was desirable that we should have a medical man to make visits of inspection and report all necessary improvements. I appointed Dr. Bryce after a good deal of consideration, and I have no doubt from the experience we have already had with him that he is a very efficient officer. I am sorry to say that up to the present time, he has not had very much time for the Indian Department. This of course is the busy season with the Immigration Department, and as he has had to reorganize a system of thorough medical inspection of the immigrants of whom we are receiving a very large number, his time has been fully occupied. However, after the busy season in connection with immigration is over, he will devote some months to im-

proving the medical service on Indian reserves. The item of $1,000 for salary is, for a portion of his salary and the increase of $1,000 in the next item in connection with travelling expenses is to pay for his travelling expenses.

I am afraid the hon. gentleman will not cure the infirmity of his appointments hy the appointment of Dr. Bryce. The hon, gentleman has been a long time in his department and he knows the Indian character very well. He knows perfectly well that nothing disturbes matters upon a reserve so much as a change of physicians. It takes the Indians a long time to become acquainted with their physician, but if they once have confidence in him then they will call upon him. If they have not that confidence they will allow their children and wives to remain without any medical assistance.
Now, the hon. gentleman has been making changes in some of the reservations, and appointing men on purely party grounds. I am very sorry to learn that party spirit has gone so far that the hon. minister feels bound to yield to the pressure brought to bear on him and to make these undesirable changes. I am personally aware that some of these changes are not in the interest of the Indians. Without offering criticism on the appointment of Dr. Bryce, I can scarcely see how he is going to remedy the difficulty the hon. minister refers to. I take the case of the appointment at Walpole Island. Dr. Mitchell was the medical attendant there. But I believe he was guilty of being a Conservative, and that was sufficient reason, in the opinion of the hon. minister, why he should be decapitated, and the hon. gentleman did not hesitate at the operation. Another gentleman was put in the position, a gentleman against whom nothing can be said. But the change meant that the Indians went on employing the physician they had been accustomed to employ. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sifton) would cease dismissing Conservative physicians he would not find it necessary to try this new remedy of his under Dr. Bryce. I would like to know in what particular he expects that Dr. Bryce will be able to overcome the difficulty that the minister himself has created. The hon. minister tells us that there is a good service. If he is convinced of that, why Dr. Bryce ? It would look a little as if the additional $1,000 for Indians is a pretext, rather than a reason, for giving Dr. Bryce an addition to his salary. It is a rather ingenious thing to divide that salary between the Indians and immigration, especially when the hon. minister tells us that Dr. Bryce cannot attend to one of them, to say nothing of giving attention to both,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The appointment to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) principally refers to was made a good many years ago
Not so many.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, six or seven years ago, and the Indians have had time, since then, to apply my hon. friend's theory and become acquainted with their doctor. I will not go into a lengthy discussion of the case, because my hon. friend and I have had it out already several times in this House. Leaving that aside, I think my hon. friend will admit that there is room for a considerable amount of systematic work in the way of improving the sanitary conditions on the Indian reserves. The question was brought up frequently in this House, especiallj last year in connection with the Brantford reserve. After that discussion I secured the services of Dr. Bryce, who was not then an officer of the department, to investigate and make recommendations as to what should be done. After considering his report and going into the matter with my officers, I came to the conclusion that we could well afford to incur the additional expense involved in engaging a competent medical inspector, who would take hold of these questions, look at them from a scientific standpoint and, with the assistance of local physicians, make regulations and provide instruction for the Indian councils. For, in many cases the councils of the Indian bands would be perfectly willing to make sanitary regulations and, to a certain extent, appreciate and carry them out. My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) shakes his head. Upon this very Brantford reserve they have a board of health amongst the Indians, and they have sanitary regulations which the Indians endeavour to carry out. But it is largely by reason of the fact that there is no competent superior officer to point out the difficulties and the means of remedying them, and also to give direction and encouragement. that better work is not done. I am satisfied that, in the course of three or four years-of course, it must be a matter of time-the difficulties I refer to would be fairly well overcome. With a competent man undertaking it

and we have the right man in Dr. Bryce-we shall make satisfactory improvement.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sifton) says the matter to which I referred has been pretty well threshed out. It is not so very long ago that this change of appointment was made, but I must say it was carried out at the very first opportunity that offered for work of that kind. I have been waiting for six years for the hon. gentleman to offer either an apology or a reason for what he did, but up to this time I have not had either. As to the sanitary condition, that is a thing much to be desired. But the hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that, while you may have a board of health, it will do no good if it is a board of health only in name. It is a very difficult matter to enforce any sanitary regulations on Indian reserves. I am well persuaded that, no

matter how laudable the hon. gentleman's object may be, he will find himself entirely helpless in the enforcement of any sanitary regulation. Those who know the Indians and their condition, realize that long after the hon. gentleman has ceased to do work in the department, there will be little change in the condition of the Indians in that direction. I had hoped that the hon. gentleman would be able to give us some more practical reason for employing Dr. Bryce- a very estimable gentleman. I may say, but that fact alone does not justify him in being placed in a service where no substantial good can be shown as likely to arise from it. Men who have some knowledge of the Indian character will expect but little to come from the scheme that the hon. gentleman has outlined. I suppose that the only thing that we can do is to assume that the hon. minister has been more upright in this than he was in the dismissal of the Tory doctors in the past.

I see that $1,000 of Dr. Bryce's salary is charged to the Indian Department and the balance to the Interior. I see also that $1,000 is allowed here, in the Indian votes, for travelling expenses. How much will be charged against the Interior for travelling expenses ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. Bryce's salary will be $3,200, of which $2,200 will be charged to the Interior and $1,000 to Indians. There will be no fixed charge for travelling expense to the immigration branch-travelling expenses will be paid out of the general vote.
You pay in travelling expenses from the Indian Department $1,000 and the balance, whatever it may be, from the Interior ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not made myself clear. The salary is $3,200, of which we charge $1,000 to the Indian Department, because, roughly speaking, 'it is expected that about one-third of Dr. Bryce's time will be given to the Indians. The vote of $1,000 is 'taken for travelling expenses. Against this vote we charge travelling expenses, *whatever they may be, in the Indian Department. If he is doing Indian work his expenses will be charged to that vote.
And if they are more, they will be charged to the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If they are more they cannot be paid, because we won't have the money. Whenever he goes away on a trip, as he constantly does go to seaport towns, his travelling expenses are paid out of the general immigration vote.

When the immigration matter comes up I hope the minister will be able to give us more reasons why the immigration requirements are put into a bulk vote, while the details are given in the other estimates. My own impression is Mr. CLANCY.
that the immigration vote should be separated into details as well as the other votes.
Indians-New Brunswick-additional amount required, $1,200.	*

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is the only supplementary item that is required, and is to pay expenses incurred last year. It arises from an outbreak of small-pox that occurred in the summer of 1903 in the town of M oodstock and the county of Carleton, twenty-eight cases in all.

Before we leave the subject of Indians, there is a matter that I wish to bring before the attention of the committee, it may be remembered that at an early stage of this session I essayed to discuss the claim of a gentleman named Jean Louis Legare. of Willow Bunch, who more than twenty years ago was instrumental, at the time following General Custer's war with the Indians in the American Northwest, in inducing Sitting Bull and his Indian band to leave Canadian territory and to surrender to the United States authorities. At that time I was not pei'mitted to make a full explanation, nor do I intend to-night to deal with this matter except in the shortest possible way. Certain of the facts in connection with this matter are indisputable. It is an admitted fact that Mr. Legare was the person instrumental in inducing Sitting Bull and his band of Indians to leave Canadian territory and go back to the United States and surrender to the United States authorities. Mr. Legare did this at large expense to himself, with much loss of time, but chiefly in the loss of a whole year's trading supplies. He was at that time a trader at the Wood Mountain mounted police post, about 100 miles south of Moose Jaw.
What was his object in acting as he did ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not want to pass my hon. friend's remarks over without ' the courtesy of a reply, but 1 simply want to refer my hon. friend to the 'fact that he has already urged these considerations upon me a very great number of times and that heretofore I have not seen my way clear to do anything in the direction which he suggests. It has been intimated that our friends are desirous of adjourning early on account of the sultry weather and if the item of civil government is passed we will adjourn.

Perhaps the hon. minister will be able to tell us how many officials he has in the inside service altogether.
As nearly as my deputy can state the number is 290.
The hon. gentleman spoke about placing some of the temporary employees on the permanent staff. I would like to ask him if any others have been put on in their places as temporary employees ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
There are no temporary employees in the hon. gentleman's department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not say that. We have not put all the temporary employees on the permanent list by any means. We have put a number of them on. When my supplementary estimates come up for consideration I will have a vote for 28 or 29 more temporary clerks who are being transferred. Under the Civil Service Act of last year you will find that the minister may, with the concurrence of his deputy, appoint any officer who is a temporary clerk to the permanent staff. We are endeavouring to work out a plan upon which that can be done satisfactorily although I am bound to say to my hon. friend that it is very difficult. We have a large number of employees all fairly efficient and to arrive at any plan whereby those who are more efficient can be picked out from those who are less efficient is not an easy matter. But my deputy has made certain recommendations which I will explain when the vote comes before the committee.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the policy of the department is to finally place all the employees on the permanent staff as far as possible ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the policy of the Act. The policy of the Act, I think fairly construed, is that these officials should not be left on the temporary list but that when the deputy has decided that their services are required and that they are not likely to be discontinued within any reasonable time they are entitled to be on the permanent staff.

I understand there are ii all the departments a large number of temporary employees wlip have been there for a number of years, who have not passed ttie civil service examinations, but who are deprived of promotion and statutory increases.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The word ' temporary ' is somewhat confusing. Some years ago the third-class clerks were abolished, but that grade is now reinstated. We employed what was called temporary clerks, but they were required to pass the civil service examination and they get a statutory increase of $30 a year. These employees were made third-class clerks. They were not temporary employees who had no fixed status in the service, but to all intents and purposes they were members of the service. However, their salaries were voted in a lump sum; and their employment was renewed by Order in Council from time to time.
